questions.q: In binary logic (as opposed to binary arithmetic), the expression 1 + 1 evaluates to:
questions.e: Binary logic must not be confused with binary arithmetic: in binary logic 1+1 = 1 (OR operation), whereas in binary arithmetic 1+1 = 10.

questions.q: A key difference between a binary logic variable and a binary arithmetic variable is that:
o: a logic variable is either 0 or 1, while an arithmetic variable may consist of many digits
a logic variable may consist of many digits
questions.e: In binary logic a variable is either 0 or 1; in binary arithmetic a variable may consist of many digits (e.g. 1+1 = 10).

questions.q: For the AND operation (x·y), the output is 1:
o: when at least one input is 1
only when both x and y are 1
questions.e: The AND truth table gives x·y = 1 only for x=1 and y=1; all other input combinations (0·0, 0·1, 1·0) give 0.

questions.q: For the OR operation (x + y), the output is 0:
o: only when both x and y are 0
questions.e: The OR truth table gives x+y = 0 only when both x=0 and y=0; the output is 1 if either (or both) inputs are 1.

questions.q: Logic gates are best described as:
o: electronic circuits that operate on one or more input signals to produce an output signal
questions.e: Logic gates are electronic circuits that operate on one or more input signals to produce an output signal.

questions.q: Although electrical signals such as voltage exist as analog values over a range (e.g. 0 to 3 volts), in digital systems these signals are:
o: interpreted as one of two values, 0 or 1
questions.e: Electric signals such as voltages or currents exist as analog signals having value over a given range (say 0 to 3 volts), but in digital systems these signals are interpreted to be either of two values, 0 or 1.

questions.q: The NOT operation (complement) applied to x = 0 produces:
questions.e: The NOT truth table: when x = 0, x' = 1; when x = 1, x' = 0.

questions.q: The two standard forms used to express Boolean functions are:
o: SOP (Sum of Products) and POS (Product of Sums)
questions.e: The standard forms are SOP (Sum Of Products) and POS (Product Of Sums).

questions.q: In the canonical forms of Boolean functions, the two types of terms are called:
questions.e: Canonical forms are expressed using minterms and maxterms.

questions.q: In a Karnaugh map (K-Map), each cell represents:
questions.e: Each cell in a K-Map represents a minterm; you put a 1 in the cell where the corresponding minterm is 1, and zero otherwise.

questions.q: A 2-variable K-Map contains how many cells?
questions.e: A 2-variable K-Map has 4 cells (m0, m1, m2, m3), corresponding to the 2² = 4 possible minterms.

questions.q: A 3-variable K-Map contains how many cells?
questions.e: A 3-variable K-Map has 8 cells (m0 through m7), corresponding to the 2³ = 8 minterms.

questions.q: When grouping 1s in a K-Map, the number of elements in each group must be:
o: a power of two (2ⁿ, where n is a whole number)
questions.e: The number of elements in a group must be 2ⁿ where n is a whole number; all 1s must be part of at least one group, group size must be maximized, and 1s can be shared among different groups.

questions.q: Which statement about K-Map grouping rules is correct?
o: groups must all be the same size
each 1 may belong to only one group
1s can be shared among different groups, and all 1s must be part of at least one group
questions.e: K-Map grouping rules: all 1s must be part of at least one group, group size must be maximized, and 1s can be shared among different groups.

questions.q: When maximizing group size in a K-Map, if a group of four can be formed you should:
o: make two groups of two instead
make the single group of four rather than two groups of two
questions.e: Group size must be maximized: for example, if a group can be formed of four, do NOT make two groups with two in each.

questions.q: When minimizing a K-Map group, which variables are selected for the resulting product term?
o: only the variables that change value
only those variables that do NOT change their value throughout the group
questions.e: For each group, select only those variables that are NOT changing their value throughout the group; unchanged variables are written as x' or x representing 0 or 1 in that group.

questions.q: For the function F(x,y,z) = Σ(2,3,4,5), the minimized expression is:
questions.e: Minterms 2 (010) and 3 (011) group to x'y, and minterms 4 (100) and 5 (101) group to xy'; hence F = x'y + xy'.

questions.q: For the function F(x,y,z) = Σ(3,4,6,7), the minimized expression is:
questions.e: Minterms 3 (011) and 7 (111) group to yz, and minterms 4 (100) and 6 (110) group to xz'; hence F = yz + xz'.

questions.q: For the function F(x,y,z) = Σ(0,2,4,5,6), the minimized expression is:
questions.e: Minterms 0, 2, 4 and 6 all have z = 0, grouping to z'; minterms 4 (100) and 5 (101) group to xy'; hence F = z' + xy'.

questions.q: A 'don't care' condition in a K-Map is a combination for which:
o: the output value does not matter, so it may be treated as 1 or 0 to help form larger groups
the input is invalid and the map cannot be used
questions.e: Don't care conditions (marked X) are input combinations whose output value does not matter; they may be included in groups (treated as 1) or ignored (treated as 0), whichever gives better minimization.

questions.q: The two equivalent graphic symbols used for NAND implementation are:
questions.e: NAND has two graphic symbols: AND-Invert, giving (xyz)', and Invert-OR, giving x'+y'+z'; these are equal since x'+y'+z' = (xyz)'.

questions.q: The two equivalent graphic symbols used for NOR implementation are:
questions.e: NOR has two graphic symbols: OR-Invert, giving (x+y+z)', and Invert-AND, giving x'·y'·z'; these are equal since x'·y'·z' = (x+y+z)'.

questions.q: For a two-level NAND implementation, the simplified equation must first be expressed in:
questions.e: For NAND two-level implementation, step 1 requires the (simplified) equation to be in Sum-of-Products form (two levels); then you draw the AND-OR diagram and replace the gates.

questions.q: For a two-level NOR implementation, the equation must be expressed in:
questions.e: For NOR two-level implementation, the equation must be in Product-of-Sum form (two levels).

questions.q: In the NAND two-level implementation procedure, after drawing the AND-OR diagram you:
o: replace AND gates with AND-Invert symbols and OR gates with Invert-OR symbols
questions.e: Step 3 of NAND two-level implementation: replace AND gates with AND-Invert symbols and replace OR gates with Invert-OR symbols. Step 4: if an input goes directly into the second level, invert it.

questions.q: In both the NAND and NOR two-level implementation procedures, if an input goes directly into the second level, you must:
questions.e: In both procedures, the final step states that if an input is directly going into the second level, you invert it.

questions.q: A combinational circuit is one whose outputs at any time are determined:
o: by the present inputs and the stored past state
by the present combination of inputs only
questions.e: A combinational circuit consists of logic gates whose outputs at any time are determined from the present combination of inputs (with no memory of past inputs).

questions.q: In the combinational-circuit design procedure, the step that immediately follows determining the number of inputs and outputs is to:
questions.e: The design procedure is: (1) specification of circuit, (2) determine required number of inputs and outputs, (3) derive the truth table, (4) get simplified Boolean functions, (5) draw the logic diagram and verify correctness.

questions.q: A half adder is a combinational circuit that performs the addition of:
questions.e: A combinational circuit that performs the addition of two bits is called a half adder; it produces a Sum (S) and a Carry (C).

questions.q: For a half adder with inputs x and y, the Sum and Carry outputs are:
questions.e: For a half adder, S = xy' + x'y (the XOR of the inputs) and C = xy (the AND of the inputs).

questions.q: A full adder is a combinational circuit that performs the addition of:
questions.e: A combinational circuit that performs the addition of three bits is called a FULL adder.

questions.q: For a full adder with inputs x, y and z, the carry output C is:
questions.e: For a full adder, C = xy + xz + yz, and S = x'y'z + x'yz' + xy'z' + xyz.

questions.q: For a full adder with inputs x, y and z, the sum output S equals:
questions.e: The full adder sum is S = x'y'z + x'yz' + xy'z' + xyz — the minterms where an odd number of inputs is 1.

questions.q: A decoder is a combinational circuit that converts binary information from n input lines to:
o: a maximum of 2ⁿ unique output lines
questions.e: A decoder converts binary information from n input lines to a maximum of 2ⁿ unique output lines (an n × 2ⁿ decoder).

questions.q: In a 3-to-8 line decoder, how many outputs are active (equal to 1) for any valid input combination?
questions.e: In the 3-to-8 decoder truth table, exactly one output (D0 through D7) is 1 for each input combination, with all other outputs 0.

questions.q: In a 3-to-8 decoder with inputs x, y, z, the output D0 corresponds to the expression:
questions.e: For the 3-to-8 decoder, D0 = x'y'z', D1 = x'y'z, D2 = x'yz', D3 = x'yz, D4 = xy'z', D5 = xy'z, D6 = xyz', D7 = xyz.

questions.q: To implement a Boolean function using a decoder, you first express the function in:
questions.e: To implement a Boolean function with a decoder: express the function in sum of minterms form, select a decoder with inputs = number of variables, connect the variables in order, and OR together the decoder outputs corresponding to the minterms.

questions.q: An encoder performs the inverse operation of a decoder, having:
o: n input lines and 2ⁿ output lines
2ⁿ input lines and n output lines
questions.e: An encoder is a digital circuit that performs the inverse operation of the decoder; it has 2ⁿ input lines and n output lines (a 2ⁿ × n encoder).

questions.q: In a priority encoder, the V (valid) output is used to indicate:
o: whether at least one input is active (V = D0 + D1 + D2 + D3)
the binary code of the output
questions.e: In the priority encoder, V = D0 + D1 + D2 + D3; when no input is active V = 0 and the outputs x, y are don't cares, indicating the output code is not valid.

questions.q: For the 4-input priority encoder shown with inputs D0–D3, the output x is given by:
questions.e: For that priority encoder, x = D2 + D3, y = D3 + D1D2', and V = D0 + D1 + D2 + D3.

questions.q: For the 4-input priority encoder shown with inputs D0–D3, the output y is given by:
questions.e: For that priority encoder, y = D3 + D1D2' (while x = D2 + D3 and V = D0 + D1 + D2 + D3).

questions.q: A multiplexer (MUX) is a combinational circuit that:
o: selects binary information from one of many input lines and directs it to a single output line
questions.e: A multiplexer is a combinational circuit that selects binary information from one of many input lines and directs it to a single output line, under the control of select lines.

questions.q: A 2x1 MUX with select line S outputs:
o: I0 when S = 0 and I1 when S = 1
I1 when S = 0 and I0 when S = 1
questions.e: For a 2x1 MUX, the function table gives Y = I0 when S = 0 and Y = I1 when S = 1.

questions.q: How many select lines does a 4x1 multiplexer require?
questions.e: A 4x1 MUX has four data inputs (I0–I3) and requires two select lines, S1 and S0, to choose among them.

questions.q: In the MUX (n−1) implementation method for a 4-variable function, the number of select lines used on the multiplexer is:
o: three (with the remaining variable applied to the data inputs)
questions.e: In the MUX (n−1) implementation, a function of n variables uses a MUX with n−1 select lines; the remaining variable (and constants 0/1 and its complement) is applied to the data inputs — e.g. for F(A,B,C,D) the data inputs take values D, D', 0 or 1.

questions.q: When building a BCD adder from a 4-bit binary adder, the central issue is that:
o: the binary sum must be converted into the correct BCD sum
the binary sum is always equal to the BCD sum
questions.e: Using a 4-bit binary adder gives a Binary Sum, which is not always equal to the BCD Sum; the design problem is how to convert the Binary Sum into the correct BCD Sum (by adding a correction when required).

questions.q: A storage element is a digital circuit that can:
o: maintain a binary state indefinitely, as long as power is provided
questions.e: A storage element is a digital circuit that can maintain a binary state indefinitely (as long as power is supplied to the circuit).

questions.q: The distinction between latches and flip-flops is that:
o: both are controlled by clock transitions
latches are controlled by clock transitions; flip-flops operate with signal levels
latches operate with signal levels; flip-flops are controlled by clock transitions
questions.e: Latches are storage elements that operate with signal levels, while Flip-Flops are storage elements controlled by a clock transition.

questions.q: In a sequential circuit block diagram, the memory element is connected to the combinational circuit in order to:
o: feed the stored state back so outputs depend on present inputs and the stored state
questions.e: A sequential circuit consists of a combinational circuit together with a memory element; the stored state feeds back, so the outputs depend on both present inputs and the stored state.

questions.q: In an SR latch, the input combination S = 1, R = 1 is problematic because it:
o: drives both Q and Q' to the same value (an invalid/undefined condition)
questions.e: In the SR latch function table, S=1, R=1 drives Q = 0 and Q' = 0 simultaneously — an invalid condition, since Q and Q' should be complements.

questions.q: In a D latch with control input C, when C = 0 the next state of Q is:
questions.e: The D latch function table: when C = 0 there is no change in Q regardless of D; when C = 1 and D = 0, Q = 0 (reset); when C = 1 and D = 1, Q = 1 (set).

questions.q: In flip-flop terminology, a momentary change in the control input C that switches the state is called a:
questions.e: The state of a flip-flop or latch is switched by a change in the control input C; this momentary change is called a trigger, and the transition it causes is said to trigger the flip-flop.

questions.q: The key to proper operation of a flip-flop is to trigger it:
o: continuously while the clock is high
questions.e: Flip-flops are constructed to operate properly when working with a proper clock; the key to proper operation is to trigger the flip-flop only during a signal transition.

questions.q: The characteristic equation of a D flip-flop is:
questions.e: The D flip-flop characteristic equation is Q(t+1) = D: when D = 0 it resets (Q=0), and when D = 1 it sets (Q=1).

questions.q: The characteristic equation of a J-K flip-flop is:
questions.e: The J-K flip-flop characteristic equation is Q(t+1) = JQ' + K'Q.

questions.q: The characteristic equation of a T flip-flop is:
questions.e: The T flip-flop characteristic equation is Q(t+1) = TQ' + T'Q: when T = 0 the state is unchanged, and when T = 1 the state complements.

questions.q: In a J-K flip-flop, the input combination J = 1, K = 1 causes the output to:
questions.e: J-K flip-flop behaviour: J=0,K=0 → no change; J=0,K=1 → reset (Q=0); J=1,K=0 → set (Q=1); J=1,K=1 → complement, Q(t+1) = Q'(t).

questions.q: In a J-K flip-flop, the input combination J = 0, K = 0 causes the output to:
questions.e: With J = 0 and K = 0 the J-K flip-flop holds its state: Q(t+1) = Q(t), i.e. no change.

questions.q: In a T flip-flop, when T = 1 the next state is:
questions.e: For a T flip-flop: T = 0 gives Q(t+1) = Q(t) (no change), and T = 1 gives Q(t+1) = Q'(t) (complement/toggle).

questions.q: A flip-flop that changes state on the transition of the clock from 0 to 1 is said to be:
questions.e: Flip-flops may respond to a positive level, a positive edge (0→1 transition) or a negative edge (1→0 transition); a positive-edge-triggered flip-flop changes state on the rising clock transition.

questions.q: A D-latch whose control input receives clock pulses is essentially a flip-flop that is triggered:
o: every time the pulse goes to logic 1
questions.e: The D-latch with pulses in its control input is essentially a flip-flop that is triggered every time the pulse goes to logic 1.

questions.q: A J-K flip-flop can be converted into a T flip-flop by:
o: tying J and K together to form the single T input
questions.e: A T flip-flop is obtained from a J-K flip-flop by connecting J and K together to form the single T input, giving Q(t+1) = TQ' + T'Q.

questions.q: A state equation (transition equation) specifies:
o: the next state as a function of the present state and the inputs
questions.e: A state/output equation (also called a transition equation) specifies the next state as a function of the present state and input.

questions.q: A state table (transition table) displays which columns?
o: present state, input, next state and output
questions.e: A state table (transition table) displays the relationship between the various states in table form, with columns for Present State, Input, Next State and Output.

questions.q: In a state diagram, states and transitions are represented respectively by:
questions.e: In a state diagram (a graphic representation), states are represented by circles and lines represent the transitions between them.

questions.q: For the circuit with A(t+1) = Ax + Bx, B(t+1) = A'x and y = (A+B)x', what determines the next state of each flip-flop?
o: the D input of each flip-flop
questions.e: Since the D input of a flip-flop determines its next state, the state equations are written directly from the D inputs: A(t+1) = Ax + Bx and B(t+1) = A'x, with output y = (A+B)x'.

questions.q: For a circuit where DA = A ⊕ x ⊕ y, the state equation for A is:
questions.e: Since A(t+1) = DA for a D flip-flop, and DA = A ⊕ x ⊕ y, the state equation is A(t+1) = A ⊕ x ⊕ y.

questions.q: In the excitation table for a J-K flip-flop, a required transition from Q(t) = 0 to Q(t+1) = 1 needs:
questions.e: J-K excitation table: 0→0 needs J=0, K=X; 0→1 needs J=1, K=X; 1→0 needs J=X, K=1; 1→1 needs J=X, K=0.

questions.q: In the excitation table for a J-K flip-flop, a required transition from Q(t) = 1 to Q(t+1) = 0 needs:
questions.e: For the 1→0 transition in a J-K flip-flop, J is a don't care (X) and K must be 1.

questions.q: In the excitation table for a T flip-flop, a required transition from Q(t) = 1 to Q(t+1) = 0 needs T =
questions.e: T flip-flop excitation table: 0→0 needs T=0; 0→1 needs T=1; 1→0 needs T=1; 1→1 needs T=0 — i.e. T=1 whenever the state must change.

questions.q: In the excitation table for a T flip-flop, a required transition from Q(t) = 1 to Q(t+1) = 1 needs T =
questions.e: For a 1→1 transition (no change) the T flip-flop requires T = 0, since T = 1 would complement the state.

questions.q: The first step in the design procedure for a synchronous sequential circuit is to:
o: derive a state diagram from the word description of the desired operation
questions.e: The design procedure: derive a state diagram from the word description; assign binary values to states; obtain the binary-coded state table; choose the flip-flop type; derive the simplified flip-flop input and output equations; draw the logic diagram.

questions.q: In the sequence-detector example, the circuit is designed to detect:
o: three or more consecutive 1's in a string of bits coming through an input line
questions.e: The specification is to design a circuit that detects three or more consecutive 1's in a string of bits coming through an input line.

questions.q: For the sequence detector with state/output equations A(t+1) = Σ(3,5,7), B(t+1) = Σ(1,5,7) and y = Σ(6,7), the simplified input equations obtained are:
o: DA = A + B, DB = x, y = A + B
DA = Ax + Bx, DB = Ax + B'x, y = AB
DA = AB, DB = AB, y = x
DA = x, DB = x, y = x
questions.e: Simplifying those minterm lists gives DA = Ax + Bx, DB = Ax + B'x, and output y = AB.

questions.q: In designing a 3-bit binary counter with T flip-flops, the input equations obtained are:
questions.e: For a 3-bit binary counter using T flip-flops, the state/output equations are T0 = 1 (the least significant bit toggles every clock), T1 = A0, and T2 = A1A0.

questions.q: In a 3-bit binary counter, the least significant bit's flip-flop input is T0 = 1 because that bit:
o: only changes when the counter resets
questions.e: T0 = 1 means the least significant flip-flop complements on every clock pulse, which is exactly the behaviour of the LSB in a binary counting sequence (0,1,0,1,…).

questions.q: A register is best defined as:
o: a type of memory chip only
questions.e: A REGISTER is a group of flip-flops; registers and counters are types of sequential circuits.

questions.q: An n-bit register consists of:
o: n flip-flops, capable of storing n bits of binary information
questions.e: An n-bit register consists of n flip-flops, capable of storing n bits of binary information; in addition to flip-flops, registers may have combinational circuits for data-processing tasks.

questions.q: A shift register is a register capable of:
o: shifting its binary information in one or both directions
questions.e: A shift register is a register capable of shifting its binary information in one or both directions; it can be used for serial transfers.

questions.q: In a 4-bit register with parallel load, the Load control input determines whether:
o: new input data is loaded or the existing contents are retained
the register shifts left or right
questions.e: A register with parallel load uses the Load input (with multiplexers at the flip-flop inputs) to select between loading new input data and feeding back the existing contents to retain them.

questions.q: A counter is essentially a register that:
o: goes through a predetermined sequence of states on the application of input
questions.e: A counter is essentially a register that goes through a predetermined sequence of states on the application of input (the input can be a clock pulse or any other input); its gates produce the prescribed sequence of binary states.

questions.q: The two main categories of counters are:
questions.e: Counters fall into two categories: Ripple Counters (flip-flop output transitions trigger other flip-flops) and Synchronous Counters (the C input of all flip-flops is connected to the same clock).

questions.q: In a ripple counter:
o: all flip-flops are triggered by a common clock pulse
the flip-flop output transitions serve as the source of triggering other flip-flops
questions.e: In a ripple counter, the flip-flop output transitions serve as a source of triggering other flip-flops — i.e. the C input of some or all flip-flops is not triggered by the common clock pulse.

questions.q: In a synchronous counter:
o: the C input of all flip-flops is connected to the same clock input
each flip-flop triggers the next one
questions.e: In a synchronous counter, the C (clock) input of all flip-flops is connected to the same clock input, so all flip-flops are triggered simultaneously.

questions.q: In the 2-bit ripple counter described, flip-flop B is triggered when flip-flop A changes from:
questions.e: The clock input for flip-flop B is the complemented output of A; when A changes from 1 to 0, there is a positive edge on B's clock input, causing B to complement.

questions.q: A ring counter produces which output sequence (for 4 bits, starting at 1000)?
questions.e: A 4-bit ring counter circulates a single 1: Q0Q1Q2Q3 goes 1000 → 0100 → 0010 → 0001 → 1000, repeating with period 4.

questions.q: A Johnson counter (for 4 bits, starting at 0000) produces which output sequence?
questions.e: A 4-bit Johnson counter fills with 1s then empties: 0000 → 1000 → 1100 → 1110 → 1111 → 0111 → 0011 → …, giving 2n states for n flip-flops.

questions.q: A 4-bit binary synchronous counter counts from 0000 up to 1111 and then:
questions.e: In the 4-bit binary synchronous counter state table, the state 1111 is followed by 0000 — the counter wraps around and repeats the 16-state sequence.

questions.q: In designing a 4-bit binary synchronous counter with J-K flip-flops, the flip-flop inputs for the least significant stage are:
o: J0 = 1, K0 = 1 (so it toggles on every clock)
questions.e: In the 4-bit synchronous counter excitation table, the least significant stage alternates on every clock, so its J and K entries are 1 or X in a pattern equivalent to J0 = K0 = 1 (continuous toggle).

questions.q: Besides flip-flops, registers may additionally contain:
o: combinational circuits for performing certain data-processing tasks
questions.e: In addition to flip-flops, registers may have additional combinational circuits for performing certain data-processing tasks (such as parallel load or shifting logic).

questions.q: In a 4-bit register, the Clear input is used to:
questions.e: The Clear input of the 4-bit register asynchronously resets all the flip-flops (clearing the stored value to 0000), independent of the clock.

questions.q: Computer 'architecture' refers to:
o: those attributes of a system visible to the programmer
the physical size of the machine
how features are implemented in hardware
questions.e: Architecture refers to the attributes visible to the programmer — such as the instruction set, the number of bits used for data representation, I/O mechanisms and addressing techniques.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an architectural attribute (visible to the programmer)?
questions.e: Architectural attributes visible to the programmer include the instruction set, the number of bits used for data representation, I/O mechanisms and addressing techniques. Control signals, interfaces and memory technology are organizational.

questions.q: Computer 'organization' refers to:
o: how the features are implemented — e.g. control signals, interfaces and memory technology
questions.e: Organization is how features are implemented: control signals, interfaces, memory technology, and so on.

questions.q: The fact that all Intel x86 family members share the same basic architecture gives:
questions.e: All Intel x86 family members share the same basic architecture (as do the IBM System/370 family), which gives code compatibility — at least backwards — while the organization differs between different versions.

questions.q: In the context of computer systems, 'structure' and 'function' respectively mean:
o: the way components relate to each other; the operation of individual components as part of the structure
the operation of components; the way they relate
questions.e: Structure is the way in which components relate to each other, while Function is the operation of individual components as part of the structure.

questions.q: The four basic functions of all computers are:
o: data processing, data storage, data movement and control
questions.e: All computer functions are: data processing, data storage, data movement, and control.

questions.q: At the top level, the major structural components of a computer are:
o: CPU, main memory, I/O and system interconnection
questions.e: The top-level structure comprises the Central Processing Unit, Main Memory, Input/Output, and the system interconnection (Computer Systems Interconnection) linking them, with peripherals and communication lines external.

questions.q: The major structural components of the CPU are:
o: registers, ALU, control unit and internal CPU interconnection
data bus, address bus and control bus
questions.e: The CPU structure comprises the Registers, the Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU), the Control Unit, and the Internal CPU Interconnection linking them.

questions.q: The internal components of the Control Unit include:
o: the data bus and address bus
sequencing logic, control unit registers and decoders, and control memory
questions.e: The Control Unit structure comprises Sequencing Logic, Control Unit Registers and Decoders, and Control Memory.

questions.q: According to the von Neumann model, any computer performs which five basic tasks?
o: reading, writing, sorting, searching and printing
adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing and comparing
fetching, decoding, executing, storing and halting
inputting, storing, processing, outputting and controlling
questions.e: In the basic (von Neumann) computer architecture, any computer performs five basic tasks: Inputting, Storing, Processing, Outputting and Controlling.

questions.q: The structure of a von Neumann machine comprises the CPU (with ALU and Control Unit), memory, and:
o: an input unit and an output unit
questions.e: The structure of the von Neumann machine shows the CPU containing an Arithmetic Logic Unit and a Control Unit, connected to Memory, an Input Unit and an Output Unit.

questions.q: A 'hardwired program' refers to:
o: the process of configuring logic components to perform a specific operation or computation
questions.e: A hardwired program is the process of configuring logic components to perform a specific operation or computation — i.e. programming in hardware, where data passes through a fixed sequence of arithmetic and logic functions.

questions.q: The main drawback of hardwired systems, which motivates the stored-program concept, is that they are:
o: inflexible — general-purpose hardware can do different tasks given the correct control signals, so instead of re-wiring you supply a new set of control signals
questions.e: Hardwired systems are inflexible; general-purpose hardware can do different tasks given correct control signals, so instead of re-wiring, you supply a new set of control signals — this is the program concept.

questions.q: In the hardware/software approach to computer components, the component that accepts instruction codes and issues control signals is the:
questions.e: For each operation a unique code is provided (e.g. ADD, MOVE); a hardware segment — the instruction interpreter or control unit — accepts the code and issues the control signals to the general-purpose arithmetic and logic functions.

questions.q: The processing required for a single instruction is called:
questions.e: The processing required for a single instruction is called an instruction cycle; the basic instruction cycle involves a combination of a Fetch cycle and an Execute cycle.

questions.q: The basic instruction cycle consists of which two sub-cycles?
questions.e: The basic instruction cycle involves a combination of the Fetch cycle (fetch next instruction) and the Execute cycle (execute instruction), repeating until HALT.

questions.q: During the fetch cycle, which register holds the address of the next instruction to fetch?
questions.e: The Program Counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction to fetch; the processor fetches the instruction from the memory location pointed to by the PC, then increments the PC (unless told otherwise).

questions.q: After an instruction is fetched from memory, it is loaded into the:
questions.e: During the fetch cycle the instruction is loaded into the Instruction Register (IR), after the PC has been used to address memory and then incremented.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the actions the processor may perform during the execute cycle?
questions.e: During the execute cycle the processor may perform: processor-memory (data transfer between CPU and main memory), processor-I/O (transfer between CPU and I/O module), data processing (arithmetic/logic), control (alteration of the sequence of operations, e.g. jump), or a combination.

questions.q: In the execute cycle, an operation that alters the sequence of operations (such as a jump) is classified as:
questions.e: A 'control' action in the execute cycle alters the sequence of operations — for example a jump instruction.

questions.q: In the simple example instruction format given, the opcode 0001 means:
questions.e: In the example: 0001 = Load AC from memory, 0010 = Store AC to memory, and 0101 = Add to AC from memory.

questions.q: In the simple example instruction format given, the opcode 0101 means:
questions.e: In the example instruction set, 0101 = Add to AC from Memory (while 0001 = Load AC from memory and 0010 = Store AC to memory).

questions.q: A bus is best defined as:
o: a communication pathway connecting two or more devices/components/modules
questions.e: A bus is a communication pathway connecting two or more devices/components/modules; it is usually broadcast, and is often grouped into a number of channels (e.g. a 32-bit data bus is 32 separate single-bit channels).

questions.q: A 'system bus' is a bus that connects:
o: the major computer components (processor, memory, I/O)
the ALU to the control unit
questions.e: A System Bus is a bus that connects the major computer components — processor, memory and I/O; single and multiple bus structures are the most common interconnection systems.

questions.q: For the data bus, the width (8, 16, 32, 64 bits) is described as:
questions.e: The data bus carries data, and its width is a key determinant of system performance (8, 16, 32, 64 bit). At this level there is no difference between 'data' and 'instruction'.

questions.q: The width of the address bus determines:
o: the maximum memory capacity of the system
questions.e: The address bus identifies the source or destination of data, and its width determines the maximum memory capacity of the system — e.g. the 8080's 16-bit address bus gives a 64k address space.

questions.q: A processor with a 16-bit address bus (such as the 8080) can directly address a memory space of:
questions.e: An 8080 with a 16-bit address bus gives a 64k address space, since 2¹⁶ = 65,536 addressable locations.

questions.q: Control bus signals transmit which two kinds of information among system modules?
questions.e: Control signals transmit both command and timing information among system modules: timing signals indicate the validity of data and address information, while command signals specify operations to be performed.

questions.q: Why is a control bus necessary in addition to the data and address buses?
o: because the data and address lines are shared by all components, so there must be a means of controlling their use
questions.e: Control lines are used to control the access to and use of the data and address lines; because those lines are shared by all components, there must be a means of controlling their use.

questions.q: The control line 'Memory read' causes:
o: data from the addressed location to be placed on the bus
data to be output to an I/O port
data on the bus to be written into the addressed location
questions.e: Memory read causes data from the addressed location to be placed on the bus, whereas Memory write causes data on the bus to be written into the addressed location.

questions.q: The control line 'Bus grant' indicates that:
o: a module needs to gain control of the bus
a requesting module has been granted control of the bus
questions.e: Bus request indicates that a module needs to gain control of the bus; Bus grant indicates that a requesting module has been granted control of the bus.

questions.q: In the instruction cycle state diagram, the stage that analyses the instruction to determine the type of operation to be performed is:
questions.e: In the instruction cycle state diagram, instruction operation decoding analyses the instruction to determine the type of operation to be performed and the operand(s) to be used.

questions.q: An instruction set is:
o: the set of registers in the CPU
the complete collection of instructions that are understood by a CPU
a list of addressing modes only
questions.e: The instruction set is the complete collection of instructions understood by a CPU; the operation of the processor is determined by the instructions it executes (machine or computer instructions), usually represented by assembly codes called mnemonics.

questions.q: Machine instructions are usually represented symbolically by assembly codes called:
questions.e: Machine instructions are usually represented by assembly codes called mnemonics (e.g. ADD, MOVE).

questions.q: The four elements of a machine instruction are operation code, source operand reference, result operand reference and:
questions.e: The elements of a machine instruction are: Operation code (do this), Source operand reference (to this), Result operand reference (put the answer here), and Next instruction reference (when you have done that, do this).

questions.q: Source and result operands can be located in which four areas?
o: ALU, control unit, bus, and clock
main/virtual memory, processor register, immediate, and I/O device
stack, heap, code, and data only
questions.e: Source and result operands can be in one of four areas: main or virtual memory, a processor register, immediate (within the instruction itself), or an I/O device.

questions.q: The four general types of instructions a computer must have are:
o: data processing, data storage, data movement and control
questions.e: A computer must have these instruction types: Data processing (arithmetic and logic), Data storage (movement of data into/out of register and memory locations), Data movement (I/O instructions), and Control (program flow, test, branch).

questions.q: Instruction sets may use how many addresses per instruction?
questions.e: Instructions may use 3 addresses, 2 addresses, 1 address, or 0 (zero) addresses.

questions.q: In the instruction representation example with a 16-bit instruction, a 4-bit opcode field allows how many distinct operations?
questions.e: A 4-bit opcode field can encode 2⁴ = 16 distinct operations; in the example the 16-bit instruction is divided into a 4-bit opcode and two 6-bit operand reference fields.

questions.q: Which of the following is an instruction-set design decision?
o: the operation repertoire (how many ops, what they do, how complex they are)
questions.e: Instruction set design decisions include: operation repertoire (how many ops, what they do, complexity), data types, instruction formats (opcode length, number of addresses), registers (number and use), and addressing modes.

questions.q: A system that stores the most significant byte in the lowest address is called:
questions.e: The byte-ordering problem is called Endian; a system with the most significant byte in the lowest address is called big-endian.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the addressing modes listed?
questions.e: The addressing modes listed are: Immediate, Direct, Indirect, Register, Register Indirect, Displacement (Indexed), and Stack.

questions.q: In immediate addressing, the operand is:
o: in a memory location whose address is in the instruction
in a location pointed to by a register
questions.e: In immediate addressing the operand value is contained in the instruction itself — e.g. with an address field of 14, immediate addressing means the operand IS 14.

questions.q: In direct addressing, if the address field contains the decimal value 14, the operand is located:
o: in the memory location whose address is stored in location 14
questions.e: In direct addressing, the address field gives the memory address of the operand; with the field containing 14, the operand is in memory location 14.

questions.q: In indirect addressing, if the address field contains the decimal value 14, the operand is located:
o: in the memory location whose address is stored in memory location 14
questions.e: In indirect addressing, memory location 14 contains the address of the operand — so the processor must make an extra memory reference to obtain the actual operand.

questions.q: In register indirect addressing, if the address field refers to register 14, the operand is located:
o: in the memory location whose address is held in register 14
questions.e: In register indirect addressing, the named register (R14) contains the address of the operand, so the operand is in the memory location whose address is held in that register.

questions.q: Given a one-address machine with an accumulator where word 20 contains 40 and word 40 contains 60, the instruction LOAD DIRECT 20 loads which value into the accumulator?
questions.e: LOAD DIRECT 20 loads the contents of word 20, which is 40. (LOAD IMMEDIATE 20 would load 20, and LOAD INDIRECT 20 would load the contents of word 40, i.e. 60.)

questions.q: Given that word 20 contains 40 and word 40 contains 60, the instruction LOAD INDIRECT 20 loads which value into the accumulator?
questions.e: LOAD INDIRECT 20 uses word 20 (which contains 40) as a pointer, so it loads the contents of word 40, which is 60.

questions.q: Given that word 30 contains 50 and word 50 contains 70, the instruction LOAD INDIRECT 30 loads which value into the accumulator?
questions.e: LOAD INDIRECT 30 treats the contents of word 30 (which is 50) as the address, so it loads the contents of word 50, which is 70.

questions.q: Given that word 30 contains 50, the instruction LOAD IMMEDIATE 30 loads which value into the accumulator?
questions.e: LOAD IMMEDIATE 30 places the literal value 30 into the accumulator, because in immediate addressing the operand is the value contained in the instruction itself.

questions.q: Assembly language is best described as:
o: a high-level language independent of hardware
the binary code executed directly by the processor
a programming language that is one step away from machine language, and is hardware dependent
questions.e: Assembly language is a programming language one step away from machine language; it is hardware dependent, with a different assembly language for each type of processor.

questions.q: Typically, each assembly language instruction is translated into:
o: one machine instruction by the assembler
questions.e: Typically, each assembly language instruction is translated into one machine instruction by the assembler.

questions.q: Machine language differs from assembly language in that machine language:
o: consists of instructions directly executable by the processor, each a binary string containing an opcode and operand references
questions.e: Machine language consists of instructions directly executable by the processor; each machine instruction is a binary string containing an opcode, operand references, and perhaps other bits such as flags. Assembly language makes much greater use of symbolic names.

questions.q: Why must an assembly language programmer understand the computer's architecture?
o: because assembly instructions reference specific processor registers, include the processor's opcodes, and reflect the bit lengths of registers and operands
because assembly runs on a virtual machine
questions.e: Assembly language instructions can reference specific registers in the processor, include all the opcodes of the processor, and reflect the bit length of the various registers and operands — so the programmer must understand the computer's architecture.

questions.q: The four elements of a typical assembly language statement are:
questions.e: A statement in a typical assembly language consists of four elements: label (optional), mnemonic (opcode/directive/macro name), operand(s) (zero or more), and comment (optional).

questions.q: In an assembly language statement, which elements are optional?
questions.e: In the assembly statement format (Label | Mnemonic | Operand(s) | ;Comment), the label is optional and the comment is optional, while the mnemonic names an opcode, directive or macro and there may be zero or more operands.

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognised disadvantage of assembly language compared with high-level languages?
o: development time, reliability/security, maintainability and portability
questions.e: Disadvantages of assembly over HLLs include: development time, reliability and security, debugging and verifying, maintainability, portability, the availability of intrinsic functions for system and application code, and the fact that compilers have improved a lot.

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognised advantage of assembly language over high-level languages?
o: optimizing code for size and for speed, and accessing instructions not available from a high-level language
no need to know the architecture
questions.e: Advantages of assembly over HLLs include: debugging and verifying, making compilers, embedded systems, hardware drivers and system code, accessing instructions not accessible from HLLs, self-modifying code, optimizing code for size and for speed, and function libraries.

questions.q: Among Intel x86 general-purpose registers, which is automatically used by multiplication and division instructions?
questions.e: EAX is automatically used by multiplication and division instructions and is often called the Extended Accumulator Register.

questions.q: Among Intel x86 registers, which is automatically used as a loop counter?
questions.e: ECX is automatically used for the loop counter.

questions.q: The Intel x86 register ESP is primarily used to:
questions.e: ESP addresses data on the stack (a system memory structure) and is rarely used for ordinary arithmetic or data transfer.

questions.q: The Intel x86 registers ESI and EDI are used by:
o: high-speed memory transfer instructions (Extended Source Index and Extended Destination Index)
questions.e: ESI (Extended Source Index) and EDI (Extended Destination Index) are used by high-speed memory transfer instructions.

questions.q: The Intel x86 register EBP (Extended Frame Pointer) is used by high-level languages to:
o: reference function parameters and local variables on the stack
questions.e: EBP is used by high-level languages to reference function parameters and local variables on the stack; it should not be used for ordinary arithmetic or data transfer except at an advanced level of programming.

questions.q: The four types of assembly language statements are:
o: instruction, directive, macro definition and comment
questions.e: The types of assembly language statements are: INSTRUCTION, DIRECTIVE, MACRO DEFINITION, and COMMENT.

questions.q: Which assemblers are listed for the Windows platform?
questions.e: For Windows the assemblers listed are MASM (Microsoft Macro Assembler), TASM (Turbo Assembler), NASM (Netwide Assembler) and MASM32 (a variant of MASM); for Linux, GAS (GNU Assembler) and NASM.

questions.q: In Euclid's algorithm used in the assembly GCD example, the key theorem is that for nonnegative integers a and b:
o: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)
questions.e: Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor is based on the theorem that for any nonnegative integers a and b, gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b).

questions.q: The distinction between internal and external memory is that internal memory is:
o: directly accessible by the processor, while external memory is accessed through an I/O module
accessible only through an I/O module
questions.e: Internal memory is directly accessible by the processor, whereas external memory is accessible by the processor through an I/O module.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key characteristic used to classify memory systems?
questions.e: The key characteristics for classifying memory systems are: location, capacity, unit of transfer, access method, performance, physical type, physical characteristics, and organisation.

questions.q: In the memory hierarchy, moving from registers down towards off-line tape storage, memory becomes:
o: slower and less expensive (while capacity increases)
questions.e: The memory hierarchy runs Registers → Cache → Main Memory → Secondary Storage (disk) → Off-Line Storage (tape); going up gives increasing performance and increasing cost, while going down is slower and inexpensive.

questions.q: The principle of 'locality of reference' states that:
o: all memory is accessed equally often
during program execution memory references tend to cluster (e.g. in loops)
questions.e: Locality of reference: during the execution of a program, memory references tend to cluster (e.g. loops); during a short period the processor works primarily with a fixed cluster of memory references — which is what makes a memory hierarchy effective.

questions.q: Cache memory is:
o: a small amount of fast memory sitting between normal main memory and the CPU
a large, slow memory on disk
questions.e: Cache is a small amount of fast memory that sits between normal main memory and the CPU; it may be located on the CPU chip or module, and its objective is to give memory speed approaching processor speed, cost-effectively.

questions.q: In the cache organization, data is moved between CPU and cache by ______ and between cache and main memory by ______.
questions.e: The CPU exchanges data with the cache by word transfer, while the cache exchanges data with main memory by block transfer.

questions.q: The three basic properties of a memory cell are that it has two stable states, can be read from, and:
o: can be written into (at least once)
must be larger than one byte
questions.e: The basic properties of a memory cell are: it has two stable states to represent 0 and 1, it can be written into (at least once), and it can be read from.

questions.q: RAM (Random-access memory) is classified as:
o: read-write memory that is volatile, erasable electrically at byte level
questions.e: RAM is read-write memory, erased electrically at byte level, written electrically, and is volatile (temporary storage). It has two types: Dynamic and Static.

questions.q: ROM (Read-only memory) is written during manufacture using:
questions.e: ROM is read-only memory whose erasure is not possible; its write mechanism is masks applied during manufacture, and it is nonvolatile. It is very expensive for small runs.

questions.q: EPROM (Erasable PROM) is erased using:
questions.e: EPROM is erased by UV light at chip level, in contrast to EEPROM which is erased electrically at byte level and flash memory which is erased electrically at block level.

questions.q: EEPROM differs from EPROM in that EEPROM is:
o: erased electrically at byte level (though it takes much longer to write than to read)
questions.e: EEPROM (Electrically Erasable PROM) is read-mostly memory erased electrically at byte level and written electrically; it takes much longer to write than to read.

questions.q: Flash memory is erased:
questions.e: Flash memory uses electrical erasing technology at block level; an entire flash memory can be erased in one or a few seconds, or just blocks rather than the entire chip. Notably, flash does not provide byte-level erasure.

questions.q: Flash memory gets its name because:
o: it flashes a light when written
a section of memory cells is erased in a single action or 'flash'
it was invented by a company called Flash
it operates at the speed of light
questions.e: Flash memory gets its name because the microchip is organized so that a section of memory cells is erased in a single action or 'flash'. It was first introduced in the mid-1980s and uses only one transistor per bit.

questions.q: In NOR flash memory, the basic unit of access is:
o: a bit, referred to as a memory cell, with cells connected in parallel so each can be read/written/erased individually
questions.e: In NOR flash, the basic unit of access is a bit (a memory cell); cells are connected in parallel to the bit lines so each cell can be read, written or erased individually. NAND flash is organized in transistor arrays with 16 or 32 transistors in series.

questions.q: A memory error that is a permanent physical defect is called a ______, while a random, non-destructive error is called a ______.
questions.e: A Hard Failure is a permanent defect, while a Soft Error is random and non-destructive with no permanent damage to the memory. Such errors are detected using the Hamming error correcting code.

questions.q: Memory errors are detected and corrected using which code?
questions.e: Memory errors (hard failures and soft errors) are detected using the Hamming error correcting code.

questions.q: The key advantage of Synchronous DRAM (SDRAM) over conventional DRAM is that:
o: it stores two bits per cell
its access is synchronized with an external clock, so the CPU knows when data will be ready and does not have to wait
questions.e: In SDRAM, access is synchronized with an external clock; because SDRAM moves data in time with the system clock, the CPU knows when the data will be ready and can do something else instead of waiting (as it must with conventional DRAM).

questions.q: DDR SDRAM improves on SDRAM by:
o: sending data twice per clock cycle, on both the rising and falling edges
questions.e: SDRAM can only send data once per clock; Double-Data-Rate SDRAM can send data twice per clock cycle — on the rising edge and the falling edge.

questions.q: In the traditional three-level memory hierarchy, SRAM is characterized as:
o: providing rapid access time but being the most expensive and least dense, making it suitable for cache memory
questions.e: SRAM provides rapid access time but is the most expensive and least dense (bit density), making it suitable for cache memory; DRAM is cheaper, denser and slower, traditionally used for off-chip main memory.

questions.q: In the traditional memory hierarchy, DRAM is traditionally used for:
questions.e: DRAM is cheaper, denser and slower than SRAM, and has traditionally been the choice for off-chip main memory; the hard disk provides very high bit density and very low cost per bit for external storage.

questions.q: Which of the following is a type of external memory?
questions.e: Types of external memory include magnetic disk (hard disk, RAID, removable such as floppy/Zip), optical (CD, DVD, Blu-Ray, HD-DVD), magnetic tape, and solid state drives.

questions.q: RAID stands for:
questions.e: Among magnetic disk external memory types, RAID stands for Redundant Array of Independent Disks.

questions.q: The term 'solid state' in Solid State Drive refers to:
questions.e: The term solid state refers to electronic circuitry built with semiconductors; an SSD is a memory device made with solid state components that can replace a hard disk drive.

questions.q: SSDs currently on the market use which memory technology?
questions.e: The SSDs now on the market and coming on line use NAND flash memory.

questions.q: Which is a stated advantage of SSDs over HDDs?
o: high-performance IOPS, durability, longer lifespan, lower power consumption and lower access times
questions.e: SSD advantages over HDDs include: high-performance IOPS, durability (less susceptible to shock and vibration), longer lifespan (no mechanical wear), lower power consumption, quieter and cooler running, and lower access times/latency — over 10 times faster than spinning disks.

questions.q: SSD access times and latency rates are described as being how much faster than the spinning disks in an HDD?
questions.e: SSDs have lower access times and latency rates — over 10 times faster than the spinning disks in an HDD.

questions.q: The compact disk (CD) digital audio system was introduced in:
questions.e: In 1983 one of the most successful consumer products of all time was introduced: the compact disk (CD) digital audio system — a nonerasable disk storing more than 60 minutes of audio on one side.

questions.q: The original CD is described as a disk that:
o: is nonerasable and can store more than 60 minutes of audio information on one side
questions.e: The CD is a nonerasable disk that can store more than 60 minutes of audio information on one side; its commercial success enabled low-cost optical-disk storage technology.

questions.q: The DVD can hold approximately how much data compared with a CD-ROM?
o: about a hundred times as much
questions.e: Vast volumes of data can be crammed onto the DVD — currently seven times as much as a CD-ROM. The DVD replaced videotape in VCRs and the CD-ROM in PCs and servers.

questions.q: High-definition optical disks achieve higher bit density than DVDs by using:
o: a laser with a shorter wavelength, in the blue-violet range, producing smaller data pits
questions.e: High-definition optical disks achieve higher bit density by using a laser with a shorter wavelength in the blue-violet range; the data pits that constitute the digital 1s and 0s are therefore smaller than on a DVD.

questions.q: In an SSD architecture, which component sits between the host interface and the flash memory components?
o: the controller (with addressing, data buffer/cache and error correction)
questions.e: The SSD architecture shows an interface to the host system, then a controller providing addressing, data buffer/cache and error correction, connected to the flash memory components.

questions.q: Optical external memory types include:
questions.e: Optical external memory includes CD, DVD, Blu-Ray and HD-DVD; magnetic disk types include hard disk, RAID and removable media (floppy, Zip).

questions.q: Why are peripherals not connected directly to the system bus?
o: because the system bus has no address lines
because peripherals are always faster than the CPU
because of the wide variety of peripherals with different operating methods, mismatched data transfer rates, and different data formats and word lengths
questions.e: Peripherals are not connected directly because: there is a wide variety of peripherals with various methods of operation (impractical to put all control logic in the processor); peripheral data rates are often much slower (and sometimes faster) than memory/processor; and peripherals often use different data formats and word lengths.

questions.q: An external device connected to an I/O module is commonly referred to as a:
questions.e: An external device connected to an I/O module is often referred to as a peripheral device, or simply as a peripheral.

questions.q: The generic model of an I/O module shows it connected to the processor by which three buses?
o: serial bus, parallel bus and optical bus
input bus, output bus and clock bus
address bus, data bus and control bus
memory bus, cache bus and disk bus
questions.e: The generic model of an I/O module shows it connected via the Address Bus, Data Bus and Control Bus, with peripheral devices attached on the other side.

questions.q: The three main blocks shown in the external device block diagram are:
questions.e: The external device block diagram shows control logic (receiving control signals from the I/O module), a buffer (for data bits to and from the I/O module), and a transducer (converting data to/from the environment), plus a status signal to the I/O module.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the major functions of an I/O module?
questions.e: The major functions/requirements of an I/O module fall into these categories: Control & Timing, Processor Communication, Device Communication, Data Buffering, and Error Detection.

questions.q: Why does an I/O module need to perform data buffering?
o: because the data transfer rates of peripherals differ greatly from those of memory and the processor
questions.e: Data buffering is a major I/O module function; it is needed because peripheral transfer rates are often much slower (and sometimes faster) than those of memory or the processor, so the mismatch must be managed.

questions.q: The three input/output techniques are:
o: programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O and Direct Memory Access (DMA)
questions.e: The three Input/Output techniques are: Programmed I/O, Interrupt-driven I/O, and Direct Memory Access (DMA).

questions.q: An I/O module contains which kinds of registers on its system-bus interface side?
questions.e: The I/O module diagram shows, on the system bus side, Data Registers and Status/Control Registers, connected through I/O logic to the external device interface logic.

questions.q: The 'Error Detection' function of an I/O module exists to:
o: detect and report errors arising in the transfer or in the peripheral device
questions.e: Error detection is one of the five major I/O module functions (along with control & timing, processor communication, device communication and data buffering), responsible for detecting and reporting transmission or device errors.

questions.q: A peripheral whose data transfer rate is much faster than that of memory or the processor would, if connected directly:
o: lead to inefficiencies if the mismatch is not properly managed
questions.e: The data transfer rate of some peripherals is faster than that of memory or the processor; this mismatch would lead to inefficiencies if not managed properly — one of the reasons peripherals connect through an I/O module.

questions.q: The 'transducer' in an external device is responsible for:
o: converting data between the device's physical form in the environment and electrical signals
questions.e: In the external device block diagram, the transducer handles the data that is device-unique to and from the environment, converting between the environmental form and the electrical data handled by the buffer and control logic.

questions.q: Within an I/O module, 'Processor Communication' as a function involves:
o: exchanging commands, status information and data with the processor over the system bus
questions.e: Processor Communication is one of the I/O module's major functions: the module must exchange commands, status information and data with the processor across the system bus (while Device Communication handles the peripheral side).
